bank.keyText: Metaphase, held by balanced pull from microtubules reaching to each pole
choiceTexts: Telophase, held by the two nuclear envelopes that are reassembling nearby

Prophase, held together by a nuclear envelope that has not yet broken down

answer.text: Metaphase, held by balanced pull from microtubules reaching to each pole
answer.line: One tight line in the middle, gripped from both sides, is metaphase. Equal pull from the two poles holds it there.

steps: Read the scene the stem describes. One tight line across the middle is the metaphase plate.
Gripped from both sides means each chromosome's two kinetochores are hooked to microtubules from opposite poles.
The two pulls come out even, so the line holds. The spindle checkpoint waits for exactly this before anaphase starts.

choices.text: Telophase, held by the two nuclear envelopes that are reassembling nearby
choices.note: In telophase the chromosomes sit at the two poles and unwind while envelopes re-form. Nothing is lined up in the middle.

choices.text: Interphase, held by the cell plate that is forming across the equator
choices.note: Interphase chromatin is too loose to see as separate chromosomes. A cell plate belongs to plant cytokinesis, after mitosis.

choices.text: Prophase, held together by a nuclear envelope that has not yet broken down
choices.note: Prophase chromosomes condense but sit scattered inside the nucleus, with nothing gripping them yet.

choices.text: Metaphase, held by balanced pull from microtubules reaching to each pole
choices.note: Balanced pull from both poles: the metaphase plate.

choices.text: Anaphase, held in place by the contractile ring forming around the equator
choices.note: In anaphase the sisters have left the middle, so you would see two groups moving apart. The contractile ring belongs to animal cytokinesis.

lockIt: One line, pulled evenly from both poles: metaphase.

Metaphase is outlined as the answer.
